name: allyourbase
title: All Your Base Are Belong To Us
provenance: Mistranslated dialogue from Zero Wing (Toaplan, 1989), a Japanese arcade shoot-'em-up; the line entered English via a rushed 1992 European Sega Genesis localization. It stayed a private joke among players until a Flash loop by "Bad_CRC" recut the cutscene over dance music in 2000–2001 and it spread across Something Awful, Fark, and Usenet.
medium: mistranslated dialogue, recut into a looping Flash animation
tradition: The purest readymade on this floor: nothing here was written for the meme. Its entire artwork is an act of recontextualization — an existing bad translation, framed and re-presented until the frame became the point, in the manner of Duchamp signing a urinal. It is the direct ancestor of the copypasta and the "it's so bad it's good" register that runs through the rest of this museum.
reception: Widely cited — by name — as one of the first pieces of media the press and early meme scholars (Limor Shifman among them) pointed to when trying to explain "internet meme" to an audience who had never heard the phrase. It escaped the screen entirely in 2007, spray-painted onto a Boston railway sign, a minor local controversy almost immediately eclipsed by that same city's Mooninite bomb scare — a footnote inside a footnote.
imageCredit: Zero Wing (Toaplan, 1989) game screenshot, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: rickroll
title: The Rickroll
provenance: Grew out of "duckrolling" on 4chan's /b/ in 2006 — mislabeled links that led to a picture of a duck on wheels — before the payload settled permanently on the video for Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up" (1987) in early 2007.
tradition: A participatory prank with no fixed object — the exhibit is not the song, it's the trap, and the trap only exists at the moment of the click. It belongs to the oral-joke tradition of the bait-and-switch and the chain letter more than to any visual meme lineage; nothing is drawn, filmed, or captioned, only mislabeled.
reception: Rare among this collection for a subject who outlived and ultimately profited from the joke rather than being erased by it: Rick Astley rickrolled the crowd himself at the 2008 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, and in 2023 performed a surprise live set disguised inside a Blink-182 Coachella set — an artist knowingly re-enacting his own meme, eighteen years after the fact, to an audience in on it.
imageCredit: Frame from the "Never Gonna Give You Up" music video (RCA), via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: trollface
title: Trollface
provenance: Drawn in MS Paint by Carlos "Whynne" Ramirez as the final panel of a rage comic titled "Coolface," posted to DeviantArt in 2008.
tradition: Descends from the rage-comic school, which prized deliberately crude MS Paint drawing as a kind of honesty — bad line art as a refusal of craft, the same impulse that runs from folk cartooning through to the stick figures of early webcomics.
reception: Became so ubiquitous, so quickly, that it was treated as public property for years before Ramirez formally asserted copyright and began licensing it around 2015 — an unusual case of an author having to reclaim authorship from a commons his own drawing built.
imageCredit: Original drawing by Carlos "Whynne" Ramirez, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: loss
title: Loss.jpg
provenance: The final panel of a Ctrl+Alt+Del strip by Tim Buckley, in a 2008 storyline about a miscarriage — quickly abstracted by readers into its bare composition: a doorway, two standing figures, one seated.
medium: four-panel webcomic, reduced to four lines
tradition: The most minimalist entry in the collection: the meme is not the comic, only its silhouette, reproducible as literally four vertical strokes. It sits closer to conceptual art's instructions-as-artwork — Sol LeWitt's wall drawings, executed by anyone from a diagram — than to any comic tradition, arrived at involuntarily by an audience rather than intentionally by an artist.
reception: Its reducibility is also its longevity: because the reference only needs four lines to land, it has been smuggled into license plates, subway maps, and corporate earnings decks for over fifteen years with no image required at all — likely the most format-portable object in this building.
imageCredit: Panel from Tim Buckley's Ctrl+Alt+Del, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: successkid
title: Success Kid
provenance: A photograph taken by Laney Griner of her son Sammy clenching sand on a beach in 2007; captioned and recirculated as an "advice animal" macro from around 2008, peaking virally in 2011.
tradition: A textbook advice-animal macro — white Impact-font text with a black stroke, laid over a stranger's unposed photo — a format standardized enough by this point that it functioned like a poetic meter: any face could be scanned into it and made to speak.
reception: Unusual among memes for how literally its goodwill converted to cash: the family has used the image's fame more than once for real fundraising, most notably a widely shared appeal to cover a kidney transplant for Sammy's father, boosted specifically because strangers already trusted the toddler's face.
imageCredit: Photo by Laney Griner, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: badluckbrian
title: Bad Luck Brian
provenance: A yearbook-style photo of Kyle Craven, submitted by a friend to Reddit in January 2012 with the caption "Takes the SATs... Sets the curve."
tradition: The advice-animal macro's structural opposite number to Success Kid: where that format's caption reads as triumph, this one reads as escalating misfortune — an unplanned matched pair spanning the format's two available emotional registers.
reception: A rare case where the fictional persona swallowed the real person almost entirely: most engagement is with an invented character called "Brian" who suffers none of the described disasters, while Craven himself has said, repeatedly and on the record, that his actual life has been ordinary and mostly fine.
imageCredit: Yearbook photo of Kyle Craven, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: nyancat
title: Nyan Cat
provenance: Built from a 2005 pixel drawing ("Pop Tart Cat") by Christopher "Prguitarman" Torres, animated as a looping GIF by the YouTube user saraj00n and set to a sped-up clip of Momoiro Clover's "Nyanyanyanyanyanyanya!" in April 2011.
medium: looping pixel-art GIF with chiptune loop
tradition: Built by synthesis rather than remix — a pre-existing drawing and a pre-existing song, neither made for the other, spliced together in the spirit of sample-based mashup culture. Its rainbow trail, with no beginning or end drawn, formalizes the "eternal GIF" as a genre of its own.
reception: The most institutionally decorated exhibit in this building before it ever got here: it was the subject of a 2013 copyright lawsuit against an app that cloned the character, was folded into internet-culture surveys held by real museums, and now has an ongoing NFT and licensing afterlife — one of the only pieces on this floor with an actual paper trail through courts and collections.
imageCredit: Frame from the GIF, based on Christopher "Prguitarman" Torres's drawing, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: thisisfine
title: This Is Fine
provenance: Panels from Gunshow #648, a webcomic strip by KC Green published January 2013, showing a dog sitting in a burning room saying "This is fine."
medium: two panels excerpted from a longer webcomic
tradition: Like Loss, its meme life is a fragment quoted out of context — but unlike Loss it keeps its original dialogue verbatim rather than reducing to pure shape, functioning less like an icon and more like a proverb: a saying repeated whole rather than abstracted.
reception: Became the default visual shorthand for institutional or personal denial broadly enough to be redrawn wholesale during real news cycles — wildfires, software outages, earnings calls — with Green noting, more than once, a two-panel joke outgrowing the 900-page career he built around it.
imageCredit: Panel from KC Green's Gunshow, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: doge
title: Doge
provenance: A photograph of a Shiba Inu named Kabosu, taken by her owner Atsuko Sato in Japan in 2010; captioned into the now-canonical broken-English format by Tumblr and Reddit users starting in 2013.
tradition: Extends the advice-animal macro into a grammar of its own: the fractured, Comic-Sans "internal monologue" register — "such X, much Y, very Z, wow" — reads almost as a constructed pidgin, a deliberately broken dialect briefly legible across the entire English-speaking internet at once.
reception: The only exhibit here with its own market capitalization: Dogecoin, launched in December 2013 partly as a joke cryptocurrency wearing Kabosu's face, later boosted into the billions by Elon Musk's tweets. Kabosu herself received a Guinness World Record and, after her death in 2024, a memorial statue crowdfunded by the Dogecoin community — bronzed before this museum ever got the chance.
imageCredit: Photo of Kabosu by Atsuko Sato, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: pepe
title: Pepe the Frog
provenance: A character created by Matt Furie for the comic Boy's Club in 2005; individual panels began circulating as reaction images around 2008, with variants (Sad Frog, Smug Frog, Feels Good Man) multiplying for years after.
medium: comic panel, endlessly redrawn reaction image
tradition: The clearest case on this floor of readymade-as-folk-property: Furie drew one character, and an uncredited, decentralized internet drew several thousand variants of him — a genuinely enormous body of derivative folk art closer to a mutating oral ballad than to any single-author work.
reception: Also the starkest case study here in meaning outrunning intent: in 2015–2016 the character was adopted as a hate symbol by extremist online communities, entered the ADL's hate symbol database in 2016, and was publicly, painfully disowned by Furie — who killed the character in a 2017 strip and produced the 2020 documentary "Feels Good Man" about reclaiming him. Displayed here not despite that history but because it is the plainest proof in this building that a meme's critical reception can invert its own author's intent.
imageCredit: Panel by Matt Furie, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.

name: distractedboyfriend
title: Distracted Boyfriend
provenance: A stock photograph shot by Antonio Guillem in 2015 for ordinary stock-agency licensing; picked up and labeled as a three-way comparison template starting in mid-2017.
tradition: The most purely structural template in the collection: a found stock image — itself already a genre built on generic reproducibility — repurposed as a reusable three-figure relationship (the looker, the looked-at, the ignored). One step more abstract than All Your Base: here even the photographed content is disposable, only the relationship between the three figures survives reuse.
reception: Recognized outside internet culture faster than almost anything else here — the European Parliament's official account used it, unlabeled, in a 2018 post about EU unity — while its three human subjects, professional stock models, stayed largely anonymous throughout: the exact inverse of Success Kid, whose identified subject cashed in on being known.
imageCredit: Stock photo by Antonio Guillem, via Wikipedia — used here, as on Wikipedia, for identification alongside commentary.
